summary: The note describes the status of Spanish in the United States. English is the dominant language of business, education, government, media and public life, and the U.S. has no de jure official language, though New Mexico provides bilingual official notices. Spanish is the most widely taught non-English language in American schools and universities, and the note gives several speaker counts, which it does not fully reconcile. It also notes that the U.S. has its own Academy of the Spanish Language.
one_line: Overview of Spanish's status in the United States, covering English dominance, Spanish teaching and enrollment, and the country's large Spanish-speaking population.
key_facts: The United States has no de jure official language, but English is the dominant language of business, education, government, religion, media, culture, civil society, and the public sphere.
Virtually all state and federal government agencies and large corporations use English as their internal working language, especially at the management level.
New Mexico provides bilingual legislated notices and official documents in Spanish and English, and in other commonly used languages.
By 2015, there was a trend that most Americans and American residents of Hispanic descent speak only English in the home.
Spanish is the most widely taught non-English language in American secondary schools and institutions of higher education.
In autumn 2002, more than 1.4 million university students were enrolled in language courses, and Spanish accounted for 53 percent of them.
In the same autumn 2002 enrollment data, French had 14.4%, German 7.1%, Italian 4.5%, American Sign Language 4.3%, Japanese 3.7%, and Chinese 2.4%.
The note states that forty-five million Hispanic and Latino Americans speak Spanish as their first, second or heritage language.
The note states there are six million Spanish language students in the United States, making Spanish the second most spoken language of the United States.
The note states the United States has over 50 million native and second-language Spanish speakers, the second largest Spanish-speaking population in the world after Mexico.
The note states Spanish is spoken as a native tongue by 41 million people, plus an additional 11 million fluent second-language speakers.
About half of American Spanish speakers assessed themselves as speaking English "very well" in the 2000 U.S. Census.
The United States is among the Spanish-speaking countries that has its own Academy of the Spanish Language.
